guide.title: Read this as a consistency-boundary design, not as a question of whether the database or the queue should be written first.
guide.problem: Service A must update its own record and ask Service B to create another one. Database commit and broker publish are two independent writes, so either ordering leaves a crash window in which one succeeds and the other does not.
guide.core_idea: Commit the business change and an outbox event in one local database transaction. A relay publishes that durable event later; Service B processes duplicates safely by recording the event ID and its business update in one local transaction.
guide.outcome: The design removes the lost-event window without a distributed transaction. It deliberately provides at-least-once delivery, then turns duplicates into harmless retries and models payment, inventory and shipping as explicit order-state transitions with compensating actions.
takeaways: No ordering of two independent writes makes a dual write atomic. Database-first can lose the notification; broker-first can expose an event for a business change that never commits.
The outbox relay is allowed to publish twice. A crash after broker acknowledgement but before marking the row published makes duplicate delivery unavoidable, so consumers must be idempotent.
Inbox deduplication and the consumer's business update belong in the same local transaction. Checking an event ID before that transaction only creates another check-then-act race.
Outbox solves transport reliability, not business sequencing. A Saga or state machine defines which event may move an order from PAYMENT_PENDING to PAID, RESERVED, SHIPPED or a compensating state.
Return the state that is already durable. An asynchronous checkout should normally return an order ID and a pending status, not claim that the entire workflow has finished.
review_lenses: Atomicity: identify every place that writes a database and calls an external system in one logical operation.
Duplicate safety: define the stable event ID, business uniqueness key and transaction boundary at every consumer.
Ordering: decide whether events require per-aggregate ordering and how stale or out-of-order transitions are rejected.
Operations: specify relay lag, retry policy, poison-event handling, retention, reconciliation and alerts before production.
